searchText: Maybe Im misunderstanding but by "doing it right" do you mean for the chain to instill a one-size-fits-all auth contract instead of the developers of various invoker contracts? Invokers can still add their own flair. It would be the union of chain restrictions and invoker restrictions. For examples, invokers can require their commit to have a time range. But the auth precompile can also require the commit to not be in a revocation list. so it's the union, only commits with a valid time range and that haven't been revoked can be used by that invoker on that chain. The precompile can also refuse to grant auth to a list of invokers with a similar lookup. Can the precompile refuse to honor the signature to a list of generic recipients instead of specifically invokers? This would be a very, very technically elegant way to mitigate the risk of malicious EOAs *and* contracts *and* invokers harming ordinary users............ The precompile can do whatever it wants with whatever context it keeps. The auth could concievably be conditional to a small set of invokers (who calls the precompile) and receivers (the target of authcall). It could keep state on-chain or off-chain. Authorization could be stored in the precompile's transient memory and the implementation of the AUTHCALL could simply look at the transient variable instead of tracking a new auth field. (the specific slot in the transient storage serves that role). I don’t think it can work within a precompile though? Aren’t they supposed to be along the lines of pure functions (or stateless might be a better word?). Auth requires playing around in the stack L2s have a lot of "system" contracts, and the new beacon chain contract also breaks that. Precompile has a mixed meaning in that regrard, between a "pure" and system contract.
